subject: Designing an occupancy study with "nebulous seasons"

messages.author: 738d983729adbc9d
messages.subject: Designing an occupancy study with "nebulous seasons"
parts:
Hello all,

My student and I are designing a study of dynamic occupancy for a woodpecker species.  We would like to assess prob of occupancy, colonization and extinction of certain habitat types between seasons (and possibly between years) by sampling each survey point twice in the breeding season and twice in the non-breeding season (and then replicating this in a second year).  I am used to working with species that have relatively defined breeding and non-breeding seasons, and from our reading, it seems that this WP species is territorial in both seasons, but can also be somewhat nomadic and start migrating at any time in the spring (though most wait until late April).   

My question is how best to design the study with regard to the timing of surveys.  Can we just sample consistently across seasons, once all 150 points are sampled, start again for round 2, from Feb though July.  OR, Should we not survey during the times generally thought to be peak migration?  Each survey is broken down into 4 periods so we can estimate detection prob from one survey and only assume closure within a survey (not between), so I suspect this is ok, but wanted some feedback if possible.

Thanks so much in advance for your thoughts.

Lesley Bulluck

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Designing an occupancy study with "nebulous seasons"
parts:
I would add that designing your survey to maximize detection of your species is always a good thing.  People conduct point counts within 5 hours of sunrise because that's when songbirds vocalize the most during the breeding season.  You could sample beyond the morning, and model time since sunrise as a detection covariate, but then there will be more uncertainty about the state process for sites with late surveys.  If those are the data you have, that's one thing, but if you have control over the design then there are better choices to be made.

Regarding your design, Lesley, the date of surveys could be modeled to account for migration, but it would certainly be better to avoid this additional uncertainty if you had the choice.  Another good resource for this topic is Nichols et al. 2009 (below) where they discuss the components of the observation process for birds, which are more complex than some folks appreciate.  Many would agree that availability is the trickiest problem for point counts and you need to understand how your survey design addresses it (e.g., plot size, temporal replication, etc.).

Nichols, J. D., L. Thomas, and P. B. Conn.  2009.  Inferences about landbird abundance from count data: Recent advances and future directions.  Pages 201-235 in D. L. Thomson, E. G. Cooch, and M. J. Conroy, editors.  Modeling Demographic Processes in Marked Populations.  Springer, New York.
